label: Existence and Uniqueness
notes: This chapter spans printed pages 503 through 548 and asks two questions about symplectic forms. Existence asks which closed manifolds carry a symplectic structure at all, while uniqueness asks how many deformation classes survive once the cohomology class is fixed. Invariants organize both answers.

label: What a Symplectic Form Demands
notes: A symplectic form is a closed two-form whose top power never vanishes. Closedness gives a de Rham cohomology class, and nondegeneracy forces that class to have nonzero top self-intersection. We read these two algebraic demands as the source of every necessary condition that follows.

label: Necessary Conditions
notes: Four necessary conditions follow immediately. The manifold must be even dimensional, it must be orientable through the volume form, it must possess a degree two cohomology class with nonzero top power, and it must admit a compatible almost complex structure. Each is necessary but none alone suffices.

label: The Implication Chain
notes: The implications run one way only. Admitting a symplectic form forces an almost complex structure, which forces an even dimensional orientable manifold. The reverse arrows fail. The chapter is largely the study of the gaps between these classes, where topology stops controlling symplectic existence.

label: Almost Complex Is Not Enough
notes: The strict gap is the heart of the chapter. Many manifolds admit an almost complex structure and the required cohomology class yet carry no symplectic form. In dimension four Taubes constraints rule out candidates, showing that the obvious topological obstructions are necessary but genuinely insufficient for existence.

label: Uniqueness up to Deformation
notes: Uniqueness is studied through equivalence relations. Two forms may be diffeomorphic, isotopic through cohomologous symplectic forms, or merely deformation equivalent through a path of possibly non cohomologous symplectic forms. Moser's theorem links isotopy to fixed cohomology, so the interesting questions concern deformation classes.

label: Invariants That Separate Forms
notes: To prove two symplectic forms are inequivalent we need invariants finer than cohomology. J-holomorphic curve counts and Gromov-Witten invariants assign numbers to a deformation class. When two forms yield different counts they cannot be deformation equivalent, which is how distinct symplectic structures on one manifold are detected.

label: Dimension Four Is Special
notes: Dimension four behaves unlike all others. Gauge theory supplies Seiberg-Witten invariants computed from a spin-c structure and a metric, and these smooth invariants interact tightly with any symplectic form present. The chapter exploits this to constrain which four-manifolds are symplectic and to distinguish forms.

label: Taubes: SW = Gr
notes: Taubes proved that on a closed symplectic four-manifold the Seiberg-Witten invariants equal the Gromov invariants counting pseudoholomorphic curves. This identity bridges gauge theory and symplectic geometry. The smooth invariant on the left is computed analytically; the geometric count on the right reflects embedded J-holomorphic curves.

label: Consequences of Taubes
notes: The equality has sharp consequences. The canonical class of a symplectic four-manifold has a nonvanishing Seiberg-Witten invariant, so manifolds with vanishing invariants, such as connected sums with both pieces having positive second Betti number, admit no symplectic form despite passing every classical obstruction test.

label: Examples and Non-Examples
notes: Concrete cases anchor the theory. Kahler surfaces and many symplectic fibrations exist, while the connected sum of three copies of complex projective plane admits an almost complex structure yet no symplectic form. These examples show the topological and symplectic worlds diverging exactly where invariants disagree.

label: Synthesis
notes: The chapter assembles an atlas indexed by invariants. Topological data gives necessary conditions, J-holomorphic and Gromov-Witten counts distinguish deformation classes, and in dimension four Taubes ties Seiberg-Witten theory to curve counts. Existence and uniqueness become questions about which invariants survive deformation and which obstruct it.
